titolo: Archegos – How One Man Lost $20 Billion in Days
descrizione:
In March 2021, Archegos Capital Management, the family office of former hedge fund manager Bill Hwang, collapsed within days. Banks that had financed its giant, concentrated stock bets through total return swaps were left with billions in losses, and the fund's positions were dumped on the market in a matter of days. This documentary follows the investigation step by step: how Hwang built enormous exposure with borrowed money, how the swaps hid his positions from the market, and what happened when ViacomCBS stock turned.

We rely only on documented sources: the SEC complaint, the US Department of Justice indictment, the 2024 criminal trial, and reporting by major newspapers. We explain the mechanism in plain language and ask what the collapse reveals about leverage, disclosure rules and risk management at the biggest banks.

fatti: Archegos Capital Management was the family office of Sung Kook (Bill) Hwang, based in New York
Reports put its assets at about $10 billion in early 2021, and press accounts say it was reported to have lost about $20 billion within days in March 2021
The banks that financed it lost more than $10 billion in total, according to major press accounts
Archegos was a family office, so it was not required to register with the SEC as a hedge fund adviser
Open question: how could a firm no regulator was watching do this much damage so fast?
Hwang worked for Julian Robertson's Tiger Management and later founded Tiger Asia Management
In 2012 Tiger Asia pleaded guilty to wire fraud related to insider trading in Chinese bank stocks, and paid about $44 million
The SEC also settled a case against Hwang and Tiger Asia in 2012
Hwang was barred from managing outside money, and the firm was reorganized as Archegos in 2013
Archegos managed Hwang's own wealth as a family office
Archegos used total return swaps: banks bought the shares and Archegos received the gains or losses without owning the stock
Because the banks held the shares, Archegos's positions did not appear in public ownership filings
This allowed concentrated positions to stay largely hidden from the market and from other lenders
Banks asked for only a fraction of the position's value as collateral, creating heavy leverage
Prime brokers included Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Credit Suisse, Nomura and others
Prosecutors said Archegos's exposure reached roughly $160 billion at its peak
Prosecutors alleged Hwang built huge concentrated positions in a small number of stocks, including ViacomCBS, Discovery and Chinese tech names
Prosecutors alleged Archegos traded in ways meant to push stock prices up, which inflated the value of its holdings
The indictment alleges Hwang and colleagues misled banks about the size and concentration of the portfolio
Because each bank saw only its own slice, none saw the whole picture
The SEC and DOJ filed their cases in April 2022
ViacomCBS shares rose sharply in early 2021 and peaked around $100 in March 2021, after trading around $40 in January
On March 22, 2021, ViacomCBS announced a stock offering of $3 billion in common shares and convertible preferred stock
The shares fell sharply over the following days
Archegos's swaps lost value and banks began to issue margin calls
Margin calls demanded more cash collateral, which Archegos could not provide
On March 25, 2021, banks held an emergency call with Archegos about the margin calls
The banks were competing: whoever sold first would lose less
On March 26, 2021, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley began selling billions of dollars of Archegos-linked stock in block trades
Credit Suisse and Nomura were slower to sell and took much bigger losses
Other lenders sold on the market as well, feeding a fast downward spiral in the stocks
Credit Suisse reported losses of about 5.5 billion Swiss francs, around $5.5 billion, from Archegos
Nomura disclosed a loss of about $2.9 billion
Morgan Stanley reported losses of roughly $911 million, and Goldman Sachs said it avoided a loss
Credit Suisse's own review found that its risk management failures were serious
Credit Suisse's chief risk officer and the head of investment banking left the bank in the aftermath
Credit Suisse was later taken over by UBS in March 2023, after other troubles
In April 2022, prosecutors in the Southern District of New York charged Hwang and Archegos's CFO Patrick Halligan with fraud and racketeering
The SEC filed a parallel civil complaint
Former Archegos executive William Tomita and others pleaded guilty and cooperated
Hwang's trial began in 2024 in Manhattan
In July 2024, a jury convicted Hwang of racketeering conspiracy, securities fraud and market manipulation, among other counts
In November 2024 Hwang was sentenced to 18 years in prison
Family offices were not required to disclose their positions in the way regulated funds are
The SEC proposed new rules in 2021 requiring disclosure of large security-based swap positions
Banks competed for fees and relaxed their checks on a client with a prior fraud history
The open question is answered: the swaps hid the exposure, no single bank saw the total, and leverage turned a falling stock into a collapse

_correzioni: Title: 'Lost $20 Billion in Two Days' is an overstated press figure; changed to 'in Days' wording (fund collapsed March 25-29, losses reported ~ $20bn in about a week)

Chapter 1: 'assets about $10 billion' is correct for early 2021; kept but removed the 'lost $20 billion within days' certainty by rewording to 'in a matter of days' (the $20bn figure was reported as lost in about a week)
Chapter 1: banks lost more than $10 billion in total: kept (widely reported ~ $10bn)
Chapter 2: Tiger Asia pleaded guilty in 2012 (wire fraud, Chinese bank stocks) and paid about $44 million: correct; Archegos founded 2013: correct
Chapter 3: prosecutors said exposure reached roughly $160 billion: correct per indictment (reported as $160bn at peak)
Chapter 4: ViacomCBS, Discovery, Chinese tech: correct; SEC and DOJ filed cases in April 2022: correct (April 27, 2022)

Chapter 5: ViacomCBS peaked around $100 in March 2021 (about $101 on March 22), after about $40 in January: roughly correct; March 22 offering announced on March 22 after close (priced March 23) of $3 billion total ($2.5bn common + $0.5bn convertible preferred): kept as total $3 billion
Chapter 6: emergency call on March 25 is correct; Goldman began block trades on March 26 morning, Morgan Stanley also March 26: correct

Chapter 7: Credit Suisse loss was about 5.5 billion Swiss francs (about $5.5 billion at the time, ~$5.5bn): kept; Nomura about $2.9 billion: correct; Morgan Stanley about $911 million: correct; Goldman avoided loss: correct
Chapter 7: Credit Suisse chief risk officer Lara Warner and investment bank head Brian Chin left: correct; UBS takeover March 2023: correct
Chapter 8: Halligan was charged with fraud and racketeering: correct; Tomita pleaded guilty: correct; July 2024 conviction: correct; sentenced November 2024 to 18 years: correct
Chapter 9: SEC proposed security-based swap disclosure rule in December 2021, adopted final rule in 2023; changed 'in 2022' to 'in 2021'
Chapter 7: 'Credit Suisse's own review found risk management failures were serious': kept (Paul Weiss report)
